utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody in and around the courtroom. And good morning to everybody down in New York. Mr. Registrar, will you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Will you please call the case, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-81-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Perisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Could we have appearances for today starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Good afternoon. It's Barney Thomas, Lorna Bolton, and Inger de Ru for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. Daniela Tasic, Chad Mair, Kate Marshall, Milos Androvic, Tina Drolec, Novak Lukic and Gregor Guy-Smith on behalf of Mr. Perisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. May the record show that the Chamber is sitting pursuant to Rule 15 bis this afternoon as Judge Picard is held up in another case. Mr. Sacirbey, good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just to remind you that you are still bound the declaration you made at the beginning of your testimony to tell the truth, the whole truth and nothing else but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. May I just have an indulgence. I'm having a technical issue, I think I've done something wrong with the computer. I just need a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You have a moment, ma'am. Will you please give her a moment, Mr. Guy-Smith. Do you need assistance, Madam Bolton?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I think I'm going to be okay, I just think I went awry in getting into LiveNote, and I just need to retrace.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If it's of any help to Ms. Bolton, I think as they say in Canada, I pass the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Guy-Smith. Madam Bolton, any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: There will be, but I still have a technical difficulty here. I'm still not to LiveNote, Your Honour. Again, if I could have one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You do have a moment, Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: Witness Sacirbey, you refer in your testimony of the 16 June as well as yesterday that you acted as representative of your country in proceedings before the International Court of Justice in relation to the case concerning application of the convention on the prevention and punishment of the crime of genocide; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Via videolink] That is correct. From 1993 to the year 2000.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: The Court adopted a resolution that you had already mentioned also on the 8th April 1993, resolution on provisional measures. And part of that resolution was quoted in Security Council Resolution 819; is that correct? Paragraph 2. Do you recall that? Resolution 819. Taking note that the International Court of Justice in its order of 8 April in the case concerning application of the convention on the prevention and punishment of the crime of genocide, Bosnia and Herzegovina versus Yugoslavia, Serbia and Montenegro, unanimously indicated as a provisional measure that the government of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, Serbia, and Montenegro should immediately, in pursuance of its undertaking in the convention on the prevention and punishment of the crime of genocide of 8 December 1948, take all measures within its power to prevent the commission of the crime of genocide. In relation to the resolution my question to you is this: In paragraph 12 the resolution said: "Decides to send as soon as possible a mission of members of the Security Council to the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina to ascertain the situation and report thereon to the Security Council." My question is this: Do you recall the countries that of permanent members of the Security Council that have been part of the mission according to paragraph 12?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Yes, I believe I do, Your Honour. The team was led by Ambassador Diego Arria, at that time the permanent representative of Venezuela, and the other countries that were represented, if I may, I may not recall all the names; but I believe it was Pakistan, the Russian Federation, France, Hungary, and I believe I'm leaving one country out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: That was my only question. I just wanted to check if you recall the members of that mission establishing paragraph 12 of Resolution 819. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Via videolink] My pleasure, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did I give you enough time, Madam Bolton?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: You did, Your Honour. I didn't do very well in computer science, I have to admit, so I'm all right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you okay now?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I am. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The witness is yours.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Sacirbey I have a few questions arising from --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sorry, I forgot about the time delay. I have a few questions for you, and the first arises from some questioning at page 7624 of the transcript, and this is in relation to a line of questioning about Resolution 713. Do you recall that line of questioning, sir?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was quite a bit of it but I do recall, Ms. Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me for a moment, I'm having technical difficulties. I can't hear Mr. Sacirbey. If he could try again, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Mr. Sacirbey, could you say testing 1, 2, 3. We are having some technical problems in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, testing 1, 2, 3. 1, 2, 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Perfect. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Sacirbey.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: All right, sir, going back to this area of questioning, there were two things that you commented on, at pages 7624 and 7721 of the transcript. You had indicated in questioning that there were states that ultimately took a view that Resolution 713 wasn't binding on Bosnia-Herzegovina, and then in questioning about this area, you gave the following response to Mr. Guy-Smith, you said: "Well, you are speaking, of course, sometimes we speak of the Security Council, sometimes we speak of the UN. As you will recall, in the General Assembly starting December 1992, there was a resolution of the General Assembly that specifically recommended that, in fact, the Security Council should, in fact, make it clear that Bosnia-Herzegovina was not bound by Security Council Resolution 713."

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I'm going to ask that document 65 ter 9090 be displayed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And sir, this is going to appear in e-court for you.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Are you able to see the document, sir?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not yet. We only see Your Honour there. There.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: You've got it? First of all, do you recognise whether this --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Is this a document of the General Assembly, sir?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. It's a reference to the resolution ultimately adopted on the situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay, if I could ask you -- I'm going to ask that we go to page, I think it's 3 in e-court. And if you could focus on numbered paragraph 7 when you do the expansion, please.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: A little more, please. Yes, we see it now. A little better focus.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sir, are you able to read it?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a little more clarity. It's large enough, but it needs more clarity. That should be good enough.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. Looking at paragraph 7, it indicates that the General Assembly is urging the Security Council to do certain things, and then at paragraph (b) it reads: "To exempt the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina from the arms embargo as imposed on the former Yugoslavia under Security Council Resolution 713." And my question is whether this is the resolution that you were referring to in cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is, and Ms. Bolton, I think it's also the context in which we were referring to the non-application of the arms embargo in respect of Bosnia-Herzegovina. In other words, it was obviously a failure to enforce international security in the context of this conflict and to that extent Bosnia-Herzegovina also had the right and the obligation to defends itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Can I ask that that be marked as an exhibit, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Its admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. This document becomes Exhibit P2617. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sir, at page 7741 of the transcript, you indicated that you had a conversation with Mr. Carl Bildt the day that Srebrenica was falling, and you indicated further that at that time he told you that neither Srebrenica nor Zepa nor Gorazde would be defended, do you recall that evidence, sir?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, Ms. Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Did either the United Nations forces on the ground or NATO defend Zepa?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I am aware, they did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Or Gorazde?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: In fact -- well, Zepa, in fact, was overrun with, as I know of no intervention on the part of NATO. To the extent the UN peacekeepers undertook any measures, they certainly were not either effective nor in any way confronted the attack. Once the attack upon Gorazde would have proceeded, in fact, at that time the evidence regarding the massacres of Srebrenica came out. And so I'm not at all certain that, in fact, the attack upon Gorazde could have proceeded as would have been envisioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. Move to a different topic, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Could I have displayed, please, I think, sir, in the binder that Defence provided to you, there was a document that was discussed and I think you'll find at tab 34 of that binder, and it -- the document ID number is ID 030648.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Should be a meeting of the Security Council 9th November, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have that in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: You may recall counsel took you to a passage dealing with UNPROFOR providing fuel to the Serbian forces based on the ostensible purpose of clearing the snow off of the roads. Do you recall that line of questioning?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, Ms. Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: This document wasn't tendered by the Defence, and I wonder if you could just take a look at it and confirm for me if this is, in fact, an official transcript of the proceedings of that date?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe this is it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If it's of any assistance, Ms. Bolton, and you would like to tender that document, we certainly have no objection.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you, I will be making that request in a moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: If I could just refer you, sir, to e-court page 7 of that document, which is page ID 030654. And looking at the -- sorry, if you would scroll up a little bit, please. Thank you. Perfect. The right-side column of this document, you'll see there's a paragraph that refers to the fact -- starts with the word: "Yesterday, as was mentioned in this council, four children and women were murdered in front of a school-yard in Sarajevo as a result of the now intensified shelling of the city of Sarajevo and its civilian population."

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I would indicate that the matter which is being discussed right now is outside of the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I simply want the witness to confirm that this is part of the speech that was delivered and this is matter that my friend -- a speech my friend went into in chief. He doesn't get to pick and choose which parts of the speech are discussed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are allowed to continue, Madam.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Just for purposes of clarity of the record, Your Honour, what I did was I showed him a particular passage for purposes of refreshing his recollection. And only for those purposes and for no other purposes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Fair enough. But it's the same document. You may proceed, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: It is. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And, sir, on that same column a little farther down, one paragraph down, what we were looking a it says: "We now find ourselves in a situation where once again Sarajevo is being shelled; our young children are being murdered on our streets; Serbian aircraft are once again flying through our skies like birds of prey." Does that speech, sir, accurately reflect the situation in Sarajevo at the time?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That's a totally different question, that speech [Overlapping speakers] accurately - excuse me - that speech may well accurately say what he said at the time, but now she is asking for an opinion on his behalf as to whether or not they were birds of prey and whether, in fact, there was any violation of the air-space at all, and in the absence of predicate facts it's improper, and once again, it's certainly outside of the scope of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: That's fine, I'll withdraw the question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: If you could turn, brief indulgence, Your Honour. Too much paper, Your Honour, I'm losing track of my place. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: If you could turn in that same document, sir, to pages in e-court it's pages 12. And in the written copy, sir, it's ID 030659. And if we could scroll to the very bottom of the page for people in e-court. You were asked --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Bolton, just a brief indulgence, I don't have that ID number in front of me. I have page numbers in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: You have, like, the small numbers, 46, 47, those numbers?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. My page -- the speech starts on page 36.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes, and I'm asking you --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before that is -- before that it is Mr. Pale [phoen], Ambassador Pale of Argentina who speaks.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Do you have page 46 a speech that follows you by the ambassador from Morocco?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I do, yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. In cross-examination, sir, do you recall a line of questioning to the effect that one of the reasons some of the United Nations member states opposed the lifting of the arms embargo was that adding more weapons to the area would simply pour gasoline on the fire?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, Ms. Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Did any countries espouse a contrary view to that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, many did.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: If I could ask you to look at page 47. This is part of the -- if we could move forward in e-court to the next page, please. Fourth paragraph down, it's a paragraph that says: "The de jure lifting of the arms embargo would be effectively implemented only in six months' time, in accordance with the proposal made last September by the Bosnian President, if the Bosnian Serbs were continuing to reject the peace plan presented by the -- if by then, the Bosnian Serbs were continuing to reject the peace plan presented by the Contact Group."

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I note that. Of course, this was in connection with the -- a proposal made by President Izetbegovic at the time, that the lifting of the arms embargo could be delayed by a few months to give the Serbian side the opportunity to accept what was then the Contact Group peace plan.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sorry --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Otherwise an indefinite application of the arms embargo would in fact in some way or another ratify the continuing military superiority at least in terms of weapons of the forces Serbian forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sorry, sir, there was a second passage I wanted to read to you before you commented. And the second passage --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: It's okay. The time delay is difficult. The second passage is then on page 48 in your copy in the next page in e-court. If we could scroll down. That's fine, thank you. Looking at the left column there is a paragraph that says: "This de jure lifting of the embargo, by putting an end the military superiority of the Bosnian Serb, could turn out to be a very effective means of dissuasion that would lead the Bosnian Serbs accept the Contact Group's peace plan." My question is: First of all, was Morocco one of countries then that took a contrary view to the view that lifting the embargo would add fuel to the fire?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, Ms. Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Can that document be marked as an exhibit, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Bolton, you gave us three ID number, ID 030648, ID 030654 and 030659. Do you want them given separate --

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: No, the entire proceedings, Your Honour, actually I think are a 22-page document which reflect the proceedings on --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Your Honours, we've lost sound from The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sorry, can you hear me now? Was I too far from the microphone?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can you hear us now?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] We cannot hear you from The Hague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You cannot hear us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Now we can.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Now we can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now you can. Okay. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] We can hear you now. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If it's of any help, the ID number of this document is 1D030648. The entire document is, as represented by Ms. Bolton, 22 pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So do you want --

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: The entire document to be made an exhibit please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: ID 030648 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Your Honours, we seem to have lost sound again. We could not hear you from The Hague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You don't hear me now? Can you hear me now? Testing, testing, can't hear me?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Hello?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Hello, can you hear us? No, they can't.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this whole 22-page document is admitted into evidence as OTP Exhibit P2618. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Can you hear us, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We can hear you, but I don't know whether you can hear us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let's get out of the movie and take adjournment. We will come back and when we are reconnected. --- Break taken at 2.44 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Mr. Sacirbey, I have just a few more questions for you. Sir, you were asked a series of questions by Mr. Guy-Smith yesterday about allegations of criminal wrong-doing on your part dating back to 1980 and the year 2000. Were you convicted of either of the incidents you were discussing with Mr. Guy-Smith?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: In fact, I've never even been charged. As it to the events in 1980, I went back and tried to refresh my memory. Actually, if I'm not mistaken, that arrest took place for resisting arrest, and I subsequently ended up initiating proceedings against the police force.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. And finally, sir, I want to go to a -- two documents you were shown yesterday. I only have to show you one of them, I think. Page 8142 of cross-examination, you were -- Mr. Guy-Smith put to you part of a document which was paragraph 19 where it was indicating that the border control authority was going to be given -- exercise its right to go wherever it wishes without any form of prior notification.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I'd like to have displayed Defence Exhibit -- I believe it was 156. Mr. Registrar, I'll be looking for paragraph 20 of that document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Looking at midway through that paragraph, sir, there is an indication that Yugoslav army liaison officer requested that the head of the sector notify him of the movements of the mission's mobile patrols in this region in order that he could provide adequate security cover. Was that requirement in keeping with what had been contemplated in paragraph 19?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That requires an opinion on behalf of this gentleman who is not able to give one, outside of -- certainly outside of expertise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Does this require expert --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm sorry [indiscernible] as a matter of fact, it may or may not, but it's certainly outside of any permissible opinion evidence and its irrelevant, and there's no foundation upon which he can make such an opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Bolton, do you have a response?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I don't believe it calls for an opinion, Your Honour. My friends put to the witness yesterday that it was contemplated that the border control would have no requirement of giving prior notification. Don't think you need to be an expert to then read or understand what has been indicated in Defence Exhibit 156 and comment on whether that is in keeping or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I see your standing, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: No, I was -- I was going to, then I stopped for a minute because you were about to speak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Then the question will be allowed. In fact, you are saying this topic was discussed yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: It was.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Ms. Bolton, I believe this was, in fact, a matter of significant discussion because it was inconsistent with the methodology that was envisioned by the provisions that were discussed yesterday. So there was an inconsistency between the theory and the application and this, of course, dealt with the application of the border control measures.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you, sir, I have nothing further for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Bolton. Mr. Guy-Smith, at the end of your cross-examination Judge David asked a question. Do you have any questions arising from that question?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I do not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I don't know if you have any questions or not, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't have any questions. You don't have --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm not asking to do anything other than as a matter of courtesy. I'd like to inform both the Chamber as well as the Prosecution that we will be moving to withdraw the appeal that heretofore had been filed with regard to the 90(E) issue because we are factually satisfied with the answers that were received, and with regard to the principle of law that exists, we don't believe that that needs any further litigation. So I'm saying that because I don't know whether or not the folks across the aisle are in the process of hurriedly trying to put together a response or not. So I want to give them that information so that they could put that into their repository of a good thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Guy-Smith. Needless to say, Madam Bolton, you don't have any questions arising from the Judge's question because you may have covered it, if you did want to, in your re-examination. Mr. Sacirbey, at long last we have arrive. Thank you so much for the time you took to come and testify. This brings us now to the end of your testimony. You may -- you are now excused and you may stand down. I hope you can find time to attend to the business you wanted to attend to today. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And thanks to all of you out in New York, Mr. Guirguis and Mr. Registrar. Thank you. You may stand down.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUIRGUIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, it's been a pleasure.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I don't believe we have another witness until Monday, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Monday is the 20th, then we stand adjourned to Monday the 20th at 9.00 in courtroom II. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 20th day of July, 2009, at 9.00 a.m. 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 3.09 p.m.
